The Colorado pikeminnow Ptychocheilus lucius is the largest cyprinid in North America, with adults attaining a maximum standard length of approximately 180 centimeters [Li = approximately 180 centimeters]. This extreme size is associated with a long lifespan, as field studies of fin-clipped individuals in the Colorado River basin have documented maximum longevities of around 12 years [am = around 12 years] at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This protracted life history is typical of large-bodied riverine cyprinids and reflects the energetic demands of a predatory lifestyle in a highly seasonal environment.

The reproductive biology of P. lucius is characterized by a relatively late onset of sexual maturity, with individuals reaching puberty approximately three years after hatching [tp = approximately three years after hatching] at a consistent temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This delayed maturation is a consequence of the species's slow growth rate and its need to attain sufficient body mass to support gamete production. The eggs themselves are small and adhesive, with an average diameter of approximately 1.86 millimeters. Based on this egg size, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0034 grams [Wwb = 0.0034 grams], a value consistent with the relatively small progeny typical of many cyprinids that spawn in warm, seasonally turbulent rivers.

In contrast to its modest birth mass, the Colorado pikeminnow achieves a truly impressive ultimate wet weight, with large adult specimens reaching 57400 grams [Wwi = 57400 grams], a value that underscores its role as the apex piscivore in the Colorado River system. This represents a staggering increase in body mass of more than six orders of magnitude from the larval stage to the fully grown adult, one of the most dramatic ontogenetic mass gains observed in freshwater fishes. The species's massive body size is an adaptation to its ecological role as the apex piscivore in the Colorado River system, where it preys upon other native fishes as well as introduced species.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] that characterize much of its deep-channel habitat, the species's development proceeds along a predictable schedule. The period between hatching and the attainment of sexual maturity, recorded as approximately 1095 days following eclosion [tp = approximately 1095 days following eclosion], involves a prolonged larval and at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]juvenile phase. This extended pre-reproductive interval is likely tied to the seasonal availability of prey and the need to survive periods of low food abundance. The yolk-sac larvae emerge from the gravel nests at a very small size, relying on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days of exogenous feeding onset.

Comparative data from closely related cyprinids suggest that the lifespan of P. lucius, which can exceed 4380 days [am = 4380 days] under optimal thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], is among the longest recorded in the family. This remarkable longevity is partly attributable to the species's low natural mortality rate in the adult stage, a pattern observed in many large predatory fishes. The asymptotic growth trajectory means that the maximum total length of 180 centimeters [Li = 180 centimeters] is only achieved late in life. The substantial investment in somatic growth, from a minute 0.0034 gram [Wwb = 0.0034 gram] egg mass at hatching to a 57400 gram [Wwi = 57400 gram] adult body weight, clearly indicates a life-history strategy that prioritizes size-mediated competitive advantage and reproductive output late in life.
